docs.description: The Economic Consequences of the Peace, written by the influential British economist John Maynard Keynes and published in 1919, is one of the most famous political and economic critiques of the 20th century.Keynes wrote this book after resigning from his position as the official representative of the British Treasury at the Paris Peace Conference. He stepped down when he realized that the Allied powers would not modify the harsh economic terms imposed on defeated Germany in the Treaty of Versailles.Here is a compressed summary of his core arguments:1. Europe's Economic InterdependenceKeynes argues that pre-war European stability relied on a highly complex and delicate economic mechanism.Germany was the central engine of this system. By destroying Germany's industrial, commercial, and transport structure, the Allies were effectively sabotaging the prosperity of the entire European continent.2. A "Carthaginian Peace"Keynes uses this historical term to describe a treaty designed intentionally to crush and permanently disarm the defeated enemy.He sharply criticized political leaders (the "Big Three") for prioritizing political vengeance and domestic election promises over economic rehabilitation and the basic food supply of Europe's population.3. The Problem of Impossible ReparationsThe book mathematically demonstrates that the financial compensation demanded from Germany was completely unpayable.He argued that stripping Germany of its colonies, merchant fleet, coal reserves, and foreign investments made it impossible for the nation to generate the trade surpluses required to pay off any future debt.4. A Prophecy of Future ConflictIn the book's most famous passage, Keynes warns that plunging the population of Central Europe into misery and starvation would sow widespread resentment.He predicted with alarming accuracy that the treaty would lead to financial collapse, social disorder, the rise of political extremism, and eventually, a second European war.

docs.description: The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) is a seminal book by British economist John Maynard Keynes. It was written in the immediate aftermath of World War I, following Keynes's resignation from the British delegation at the Paris Peace Conference in protest of the Treaty of Versailles. It is widely considered one of the most influential books of the 20th century, famous for its biting criticism of the Allied leaders and its chillingly accurate prediction that the treaty's harsh terms would lead to the economic collapse of Germany and a second world war. Keynes's central thesis was that the treaty was a "Carthaginian Peace"—a reference to the total destruction of Carthage by Rome—designed to crush Germany rather than rehabilitate Europe. Impossible Reparations: Keynes argued that the reparations demanded by the Allies (billions of dollars) were well beyond Germany's capacity to pay. He calculated that Germany could afford at most £2 billion, while the Allies were demanding many times that amount. The Economic Unity of Europe: He insisted that Europe’s economy was interconnected. Germany was the industrial engine of the continent; by crippling Germany, the Allies were effectively destroying the markets for their own goods and ensuring a continent-wide depression. Betrayal of Terms: He argued the treaty violated the terms of the Armistice, which Germany had signed based on Woodrow Wilson’s "Fourteen Points."

description: "John Maynard Keynes, then a rising young economist, participated in the Paris Peace Conference in 1919 as chief representative of the British Treasury and advisor to Prime Minister David Lloyd George. He resigned after desperately trying and failing to reduce the huge demands for reparations being made on Germany. The Economic Consequences of the Peace is Keynes' brilliant and prophetic analysis of the effects that the peace treaty would have both on Germany and, even more fatefully, the world." "A popular lecturer of economics at Cambridge University and editor of the Economic Journal, Keynes made The Economic Consequences of the Peace a major step in his career. It was translated into a dozen languages and sold 100,000 copies in six months. Taken seriously even by those who were opposed to his claims, the book helped lift economics to a new, higher level of recognition and acceptance. This volume, with its insightful portraits of Lloyd George, Georges Clemenceau, and Woodrow Wilson, remains one of the great works of political economy of our time."--Jacket

description: "The story begins with Duveen pere, a Dutch Jew immigrating to Britain in 1866, establishing a business in London, going from humble beginnings in an antiques shop to a knighthood celebrating him as one of the country's leading art dealers. Duveen pere could discern an Old Master beneath layers of discolored varnish. He perfected the chase, the subterfuges, the strategies, the double dealings. He had an uncanny ability to spot a hidden treasure. It was called "the Duveen eye." His son, Joseph, grew up with it and learned it all - and more." "Secrest tells us how the young Duveen was motivated from the beginning by the thrill of discovery; how he ascended, at twenty-nine, to (de facto) head of the business; how he moved away from the firm's emphasis on tapestries and Chinese porcelains toward the more speculative, more lucrative, more exciting business of dealing in Old Masters. We see a demand for these paintings growing in America, fueled by the new "squillionaires" just at the moment when British aristocrats with great art collections were losing their fortunes ... how Duveen's whole career was based on the simple observation: Europe has the art; America, the money." "Secrest shows how he sold hundreds of masterpieces by Bellini, Botticelli, Giotto, Raphael, Rembrandt, Gainsborough, Watteau, Velazquez, Vermeer, and Titian, among others, by convincing such self-made Americans as Morgan, Frick, Huntington, Widener, Bache, Mellon, and Kress that ownership of great art would ennoble them, and while waving such huge sums at the already noble British owners that the art changed hands and all were happy." "Duveen was as generous as he was acquisitive, giving away hundreds of thousands of pounds to British institutions (the Tate Gallery, the National Portrait Gallery, the British Museum - including rooms to house the Elgin Marbles), organizing exhibitions for young artists, writing books about British art, and playing a major role in the design of the National Gallery in Washington."--Jacket
